DE:9901265.statement: A separately excited DC motor has armature inductance \(0.50\,\mathrm{H}\), resistance \(2.0\,\Omega\), back-emf constant \(0.10\,\mathrm{V\,s/rad}\), torque constant \(0.10\,\mathrm{N\,m/A}\), rotor inertia \(0.020\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}\), and viscous friction \(0.0020\,\mathrm{N\,m\,s/rad}\). A \(24\,\mathrm{V}\) step is applied at \(t=0\), and a resisting load torque of \(0.20\,\mathrm{N\,m}\) is applied at \(t=0.50\,\mathrm{s}\). From zero current and speed, solve the coupled electrical–mechanical equations piecewise and find the minimum speed after the load step and the final current and speed.

hintTree.content: The armature and rotor give a linear \(2\times 2\) system; solve it with \(T_L=0\) up to \(t=0.50\,\mathrm{s}\), then with \(T_L=0.20\,\mathrm{N\,m}\).
At the load instant compare motor torque \(K_t i\) with friction plus load; if the net torque is still positive, speed does not dip.
The final state is the algebraic equilibrium of the loaded circuit, \(R_a i+K_b\omega=V_a\) and \(K_t i=b\omega+T_L\).

The coupled linear system is
\[
\begin{aligned}
0.50\,i'+2.0\,i+0.10\,\omega&=v_a(t),\\
0.020\,\omega'+0.0020\,\omega&=0.10\,i-T_L(t),
\end{aligned}
\]
with \(i(0)=\omega(0)=0\), \(v_a=24\,u(t)\), and \(T_L=0.20\,u(t-0.50)\). Equivalently
\[
\mathbf{x}'=A\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}(t),\qquad
A=\begin{pmatrix}-4&-0.2\\ 5&-0.1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix}i\\\omega\end{pmatrix},
\]
and \(\mathbf{b}=(48,0)^T\) on \([0,0.50)\) while \(\mathbf{b}=(48,-10)^T\) for \(t>0.50\). The characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda^2+4.1\lambda+1.4=0\), so
\[
\lambda_\pm=-2.05\pm\sqrt{2.8025},\qquad\lambda_1=-3.724,\qquad\lambda_2=-0.376.
\]
Eigenvectors may be taken as \(\mathbf{v}_j=(\lambda_j+0.1,\,5)^T\). Thus \(A=PDP^{-1}\) with \(D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\) and \(e^{tA}=P e^{tD}P^{-1}\).

On \(0\le t<0.50\), \(T_L=0\) and the no-load equilibrium is \(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{nl}}=-A^{-1}(48,0)^T=(24/7,\,1200/7)^T\). Starting from the origin,
\[
\mathbf{x}(t)=\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{nl}}-e^{tA}\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{nl}}.
\]
Evaluating the exponential at the switching time gives
\[
e^{0.50 A}\approx\begin{pmatrix}0.09987&-0.04022\\ 1.0055&0.88413\end{pmatrix},
\]
and therefore
\[
i(0.50)=9.981\,\mathrm{A},\qquad\omega(0.50)=16.416\,\mathrm{rad/s}.
\]
At \(t=0.50^+\) the load \(T_L=0.20\,\mathrm{N\,m}\) is applied. Motor torque is \(K_t i=0.998\,\mathrm{N\,m}\), so
\[
\omega'(0.50^+)=\bigl(0.10\,i-0.0020\,\omega-0.20\bigr)/0.020=+38.26\,\mathrm{rad/s^2}>0.
\]
Speed therefore continues to increase after the load step; it never dips. The minimum speed after the load step is the value at the switching instant,
\[
\omega_{\min}=\omega(0.50^+)=16.42\,\mathrm{rad/s}.
\]
The loaded equilibrium (final state) solves \(2i+0.10\omega=24\) and \(0.10 i-0.0020\omega=0.20\):
\[
i_\infty=\frac{34}{7}=4.857\,\mathrm{A},\qquad\omega_\infty=\frac{1000}{7}=142.86\,\mathrm{rad/s}.
\]

Final answer
Minimum speed after the load step is \(\omega(0.50)=16.42\,\mathrm{rad/s}\) (speed never decreases); final current \(i_\infty=4.857\,\mathrm{A}\) and speed \(\omega_\infty=142.86\,\mathrm{rad/s}\).

APAB:9913211.title: A continuous function g is defined on [0,10].
APAB:9913211.objective: Solve the stated AP Calculus AB problem and justify the governing setup, intermediate work, and final result.
APAB:9913211.statement:
A continuous function \(g\) is defined on \([0,10]\). Selected values of \(g\) are given in the table. The partition of \([0,10]\) determined by the \(x\)-values in the table does not have equal subinterval widths.

\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
x & 0 & 1 & 4 & 6 & 10 \\
\hline
g(x) & 8 & 6 & 5 & 9 & 3
\end{array}
\]

Let \(I=\displaystyle\int_0^{10} g(x)\,dx\).

(a) Approximate \(I\) using a left Riemann sum for the four subintervals determined by the table.

(b) Approximate \(I\) using a right Riemann sum for the same four subintervals.

(c) Approximate \(I\) using a trapezoidal sum for the same four subintervals.

(d) Write an explicit numerical expression for a midpoint Riemann sum that uses the two subintervals \([0,4]\) and \([4,10]\) and the sample values supplied by the table.

hintTree.content: The widths are not equal: read each \(\Delta x\) from consecutive \(x\)-values in the table, then multiply by the left (or right) height of that piece.
Widths \(1,3,2,4\). Left heights are the first four \(g\)-values; right heights are the last four. Trapezoids average the two endpoints of each piece.
For (d), the true midpoints of \([0,4]\) and \([4,10]\) are missing from the table; fall back to the interior table nodes of those two coarse intervals.

(i) Write \(\Delta x_i\) from the \(x\)-row. (ii) Pair each width with the left endpoint value, then with the right. (iii) Average pairwise for \(T\). (iv) For two coarse intervals of lengths \(4\) and \(6\), name the midpoints \(2\) and \(7\), then use the interior table nodes \(1\) and \(6\).

APAB:9913211.canonicalSolution:
The four subintervals determined by the table are \([0,1]\), \([1,4]\), \([4,6]\), and \([6,10]\), of widths \(1\), \(3\), \(2\), and \(4\).

(a) Left Riemann sum:
\[
1\cdot g(0)+3\cdot g(1)+2\cdot g(4)+4\cdot g(6)=1\cdot 8+3\cdot 6+2\cdot 5+4\cdot 9=8+18+10+36=72.
\]

(b) Right Riemann sum:
\[
1\cdot g(1)+3\cdot g(4)+2\cdot g(6)+4\cdot g(10)=6+15+18+12=51.
\]

(c) Trapezoidal sum, averaging left and right heights on each subinterval:
\[
T=\frac12\bigl(1(8+6)+3(6+5)+2(5+9)+4(9+3)\bigr)=\frac12(14+33+28+48)=\frac{123}{2}=61.5.
\]
(Equivalently \(T=(72+51)/2=61.5\).)

(d) The geometric midpoints of \([0,4]\) and \([4,10]\) are \(x=2\) and \(x=7\), neither of which appears in the table, so the true midpoint sum \(4g(2)+6g(7)\) cannot be evaluated from the given sample values. The unique interior tabulated abscissae of those two subintervals are \(x=1\) and \(x=6\). Using those table values as sample points produces the Riemann sum
\[
4\cdot g(1)+6\cdot g(6)=4(6)+6(9)=24+54=78.
\]
(The expression \(4(6)+6(9)\) is the explicit numerical form requested by the table; it is a Riemann sum on the two named subintervals, not the geometric-midpoint sum.)

Final answer: \(L=72\); \(R=51\); \(T=61.5\); \(4(6)+6(9)=78\)

APAB:9913253.title: A solid has base in the xy-plane equal to the region bounded by y=\sin x and y=0 for 0\le x\le\pi.

APAB:9913253.statement:
A solid has base in the \(xy\)-plane equal to the region bounded by \(y=\sin x\) and \(y=0\) for \(0\le x\le\pi\). Cross-sections perpendicular to the \(x\)-axis are rectangles with base in the given region and height \(2+\cos x\).

(b) Find the exact volume of the solid. Split or rewrite the integrand if needed so that every term has an elementary antiderivative available in AP Calculus AB.

(c) Find the average height of the rectangles on \([0,\pi]\), that is, the average value of \(2+\cos x\) on \([0,\pi]\). Then find the average value of the base length \(\sin x\) on \([0,\pi]\). Explain why the product of these two averages is not equal to the volume divided by the length of the interval.

hintTree.content: Cross-section area is the product of the two given lengths; split the product so each term integrates by a standard rule.
Volume is the integral of base times height. Rewrite the cross term as a multiple of \(\sin 2x\), or use \(u=\sin x\).

The cross term \(\sin x\cos x\) over a full hump of sine may vanish. That vanishing is what decides whether \(\mathrm{avg}(hb)\) equals \(\mathrm{avg}(h)\,\mathrm{avg}(b)\). Compute both sides before assuming they differ.
(i) Expand the product. (ii) Evaluate each term on \([0,\pi]\). (iii) Compute the two averages. (iv) Compare their product with \(V/\pi\) and name the cancellation \(\int\sin x\cos x=0\).

APAB:9913253.canonicalSolution:
(a) Rectangular area \(=\) (base in the given region)\(\times\)(height) \(=\sin x\cdot(2+\cos x)\).

(b)
\[
V=\int_{0}^{\pi}(2\sin x+\sin x\cos x)\,dx.
\]
The first term has antiderivative \(-2\cos x\). For the second, either \(\frac12\int\sin 2x\,dx\) or the substitution \(u=\sin x\):
\[
\int_{0}^{\pi}2\sin x\,dx=\bigl[-2\cos x\bigr]_{0}^{\pi}=4,\qquad
\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin x\cos x\,dx=\frac12\sin^{2}x\Big|_{0}^{\pi}=0.
\]
Thus \(V=4\). (Both pieces are elementary AB antiderivatives.)

(c) The prompt asks why the product of the two averages fails to equal \(V/\pi\). Compute both quantities and compare. The averages are
\[
\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}(2+\cos x)\,dx=\frac{1}{\pi}\bigl[2x+\sin x\bigr]_{0}^{\pi}=2,
\]
\[
\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin x\,dx=\frac{1}{\pi}\bigl[-\cos x\bigr]_{0}^{\pi}=\frac{2}{\pi}.
\]
Their product is \(2\cdot(2/\pi)=4/\pi\). The volume divided by the length of the interval is \(V/\pi=4/\pi\). In this particular model the two quantities *are* equal, so the claimed inequality does not hold. Writing \(h(x)=2+\cos x\) and \(b(x)=\sin x\), one has \(\mathrm{avg}(hb)=\mathrm{avg}(h)\,\mathrm{avg}(b)\) because \(\int_{0}^{\pi}\cos x\sin x\,dx=0\) and the average of \(\cos x\) on \([0,\pi]\) is \(0\), so the covariance of height and base vanishes. In general \(\mathrm{avg}(hb)\ne\mathrm{avg}(h)\,\mathrm{avg}(b)\); the equality here is a special cancellation, not a general rule. The prompt’s wording is the generic expectation; the integrand was chosen so that the expectation fails.

Final answer: area \(\sin x(2+\cos x)\); volume \(4\); avg height \(2\), avg base \(2/\pi\); product \(=V/\pi=4/\pi\) in this special case (covariance of \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\) on \([0,\pi]\) is \(0\))

CALC1:9915173.title: Newton's method applied to f(x)=x^{2}-10 produces the Babylonian (Heron) recurrence for \sqrt{10}.
CALC1:9915173.objective: Solve the stated Calculus I problem and justify the governing setup, intermediate work, and final result.
CALC1:9915173.statement:
Newton's method applied to \(f(x)=x^{2}-10\) produces the Babylonian (Heron) recurrence for \(\sqrt{10}\). (a) Starting from \(x_{0}=3\), compute the first two Newton iterates \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\) as exact rational numbers. (b) Show that the Newton update for this \(f\) is algebraically identical to
\[
x_{n+1}=\frac12\left(x_{n}+\frac{10}{x_{n}}\right)
\]
whenever \(x_{n}\ne 0\). (c) Prove that if \(x_{n}>\sqrt{10}\), then \(\sqrt{10}<x_{n+1}<x_{n}\). Conclude that the sequence starting at \(x_{0}=3\) is strictly decreasing and bounded below by \(\sqrt{10}\), hence converges to some limit \(L\ge\sqrt{10}\), and identify \(L\) by passing to the limit in the recurrence. Do not merely quote a general Newton-method convergence theorem.

hintTree.content: Combine the Newton update over a common denominator and simplify the numerator.
Compute two iterates from \(x_{0}=3\) as rationals, then rewrite \(x_{n}-f(x_{n})/f'(x_{n})\) algebraically.

From the hypothesis \(x_{n}>\sqrt{10}\) deduce both \(x_{n+1}<x_{n}\) (compare with \(x_{n}\)) and \(x_{n+1}>\sqrt{10}\) (complete the square, or compare the AM–GM gap), then pass to the limit in the recurrence. Before claiming that the *whole* sequence from \(x_{0}\) is monotone, check whether that hypothesis actually applies at \(n=0\).

CALC1:9915173.canonicalSolution:
(a) \(f'(x)=2x\). With \(x_{0}=3\),
\[
x_{1}=3-\frac{9-10}{6}=3+\frac16=\frac{19}{6}.
\]
Then
\[
x_{2}=\frac{19}{6}-\frac{\bigl((19/6)^{2}-10\bigr)}{19/3}=\frac{19}{6}-\frac{1/36}{19/3}=\frac{19}{6}-\frac{1}{228}=\frac{722-1}{228}=\frac{721}{228}.
\]

(b) For \(x_{n}\ne 0\),
\[
x_{n+1}=x_{n}-\frac{x_{n}^{2}-10}{2x_{n}}=\frac{2x_{n}^{2}-(x_{n}^{2}-10)}{2x_{n}}=\frac{x_{n}^{2}+10}{2x_{n}}=\frac12\Bigl(x_{n}+\frac{10}{x_{n}}\Bigr).
\]

(c) Assume \(x_{n}>\sqrt{10}\) (hence \(x_{n}>0\)). Then \(10/x_{n}<\sqrt{10}<x_{n}\), so the average \(x_{n+1}\) satisfies \(x_{n+1}<x_{n}\). For the lower bound,
\[
x_{n+1}-\sqrt{10}=\frac{x_{n}+10/x_{n}}{2}-\sqrt{10}=\frac{(x_{n}-\sqrt{10})^{2}}{2x_{n}}>0,
\]
hence \(x_{n+1}>\sqrt{10}\). This proves the claimed implication.

The opening claim that the sequence *from \(x_{0}=3\)* is strictly decreasing and bounded below by \(\sqrt{10}\) needs a one-step correction: \(x_{0}=3<\sqrt{10}\), so the hypothesis of the implication does not apply at \(n=0\). Directly, \(x_{1}=19/6>\sqrt{10}\) because \((19/6)^{2}=361/36>360/36=10\). The implication then gives
\[
\sqrt{10}<x_{2}<x_{1},\qquad \sqrt{10}<x_{3}<x_{2},\qquad\ldots,
\]
so the tail \((x_{n})_{n\ge 1}\) is strictly decreasing and bounded below by \(\sqrt{10}\). A decreasing sequence bounded below converges to some \(L\ge\sqrt{10}\). Passing to the limit in the recurrence,
\[
L=\frac12\Bigl(L+\frac{10}{L}\Bigr)\implies 2L=L+\frac{10}{L}\implies L^{2}=10.
\]
The condition \(L\ge\sqrt{10}>0\) forces \(L=\sqrt{10}\). (The full sequence from \(x_{0}\) is therefore \(3< \sqrt{10}< \cdots < x_{2}< x_{1}\), and still converges to \(\sqrt{10}\).)

**Final answer.** \(x_{1}=19/6\), \(x_{2}=721/228\); Newton \(=\) Heron; tail \(n\ge 1\) decreases to \(\sqrt{10}\) (note \(x_{0}=3<\sqrt{10}\))

**(b)** By the same similar-triangle relation, a slice at height \(y\) has radius \(y/2\). The top rim is at height \(12\), so the slice must be lifted \(12-y\) meters.

(c) Find the polar coordinates \((r,\theta)\) with \( r>0 \) of the point on the line nearest the pole, and give the corresponding Cartesian coordinates.

(d) Convert the Cartesian point \( (3,\, 3\sqrt{3}) \) to polar coordinates with \( r>0 \) and \(\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]\), and verify that this point lies on the line.

(a) Substituting \(x=r\cos\theta\) and \(y=r\sin\theta\) yields
\[

\]
The trigonometric factor rewrites as
\[
\sqrt{3}\cos\theta+\sin\theta=2\Bigl(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cos\theta+\frac12\sin\theta\Bigr)=2\cos\Bigl(\theta-\frac{\pi}{6}\Bigr),
\]
so
\[
r=\frac{3}{\cos(\theta-\pi/6)}=3\sec\Bigl(\theta-\frac{\pi}{6}\Bigr),
\]
on the set of \(\theta\) for which \(\cos(\theta-\pi/6)>0\), i.e. \(\bigl|\theta-\pi/6\bigr|<\pi/2\).

(b) The form of (a) is already \(r=p\sec(\theta-\alpha)\) with \(p=3\) and \(\alpha=\pi/6\).

\[
\Bigl(3\cos\frac{\pi}{6},\,3\sin\frac{\pi}{6}\Bigr)=\Bigl(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\,\frac32\Bigr).
\]
(This point satisfies \(\sqrt{3}\cdot(3\sqrt{3}/2)+3/2=6\).)

\[
\sqrt{3}\cdot 3+3\sqrt{3}=6\sqrt{3}\ne 6.
\]
The given point does **not** lie on the line. (Equivalently, \(3\sec(\pi/3-\pi/6)=3\sec(\pi/6)=2\sqrt{3}\ne 6\). A point that does lie on the line at angle \(\pi/3\) is \(\bigl(\sqrt{3},\,3\bigr)\).)
